From @pcogovph 

Inspection of the Pasig-Marikina River Channel Improvement Project Phase IV Barangay Sto. Niño, Marikina City August 11, 2025

Demonstrating the Administration’s resolute commitment to protecting communities from flood hazards, President @bongbongmarcos leads the inspection of the Pasig–Marikina River Channel Improvement Project (PMRCIP) Phase IV at the Marikina Bridge Under Loop in Barangay Sto. Niño, Marikina City on 11 August 2025.

Led by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in partnership with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), this project aims to reduce further flooding caused by the overflow of the Pasig and Marikina Rivers.

Phase IV involves both structural and non-structural measures to reduce flood damage in Metro Manila and surrounding areas, supporting urban development and encouraging a sustainable environment along the river.
Its scope of work includes constructing dikes and revetments, installing floodgates and dredging channels - improving the flood management infrastructure of the National Capital Region (NCR).
The PMRCIP Phase IV – Contract Package 3 is a major infrastructure project in the country, funded through agreements with Japan.

Video courtesy of @pcogovph and RTVM

Mayor Vico Sotto’s Bombshell on Flood Control Corruption - and How It Ties to PBBM’s Push for Accountability

This morning of August 11, Monday, Pasig Mayor Vico Sotto dropped a loaded post on Facebook that resonated far beyond Pasig. It wasn’t just a casual update - it was a pointed reaction to President @bongbongmarcos 
’ presentation of the Top 15 DPWH Contractors for Flood Control Projects.

In that list, Alpha & Omega ranked #2 and St. Timothy #3. According to Vico, both companies - along with St. Gerrard and others - are controlled by one family: the Discayas.

Mayor Vico didn’t mince words. He framed it within the President’s own SONA call-out:

“MAHIYA NAMAN KAYO!”

The Six Stages of Corruption - A Breakdown

Mayor Vico outlined what he called the “6 Stages of Corruption” in infrastructure projects. It’s a roadmap - not of progress, but of rot.
 
1. Anomalies start in procurement/bidding - possible collusion even before the first shovel hits the ground.

2. Substandard or “imaginary” projects - echoing PBBM’s SONA jab at “guni-guni lang” flood control projects.

3. SOP or kickbacks - allegedly reaching more than 50% of project cost.

4. Tax evasion on national level - contractors skipping proper BIR payments.

5. Tax evasion on local level - one top contractor reportedly declared ZERO gross revenue to Pasig LGU despite massive contracts.

6. Political reinvestment of stolen funds - using 1% of ill-gotten gains for token “aid” to look benevolent, while securing influence.

It’s a vicious cycle where corruption not only bleeds the budget dry, but also sustains political machinery that protects it.

Why This Matters Beyond Pasig

What makes this post important is the convergence of two things:

PBBM’s National Exposé: By naming top contractors, the President is breaking an unwritten code when normally, such matters stay in bureaucratic shadows.

LGU Reinforcement: Mayor Vico, from a local vantage point, is confirming the systemic nature of these schemes and pledging local legal action.

The President’s https://t.co/7HETL8KpOn initiative fits right into this wherein a direct citizen reporting channel serves to bypass the layers that protect entrenched interests.

Vico’s Two-Point Plan for Pasig

1. Send red flags to the President - This strengthens the data pool for national-level scrutiny.

2. Pursue cases to collect unpaid business taxes - A move that could fund major Pasig infrastructure without cutting other programs.

If executed, this is more than a name-and-shame moment - it’s a template for how LGUs can directly complement PBBM’s anti-corruption drive.

The Political Undertone

Vico’s note that all candidates supported by this group in Pasig (and their partylist) lost suggests that while money talks, the electorate can still reject it. It’s a subtle but strong message: dirty money can’t always buy clean victories.

This is also a moment where political lines blur a - both #PBBM and #VicoSotto are essentially on the same side here, despite different party affiliations. The fight isn’t over turf, it’s over cleaning house.

Bigger Picture: A National Shift

Corruption in infrastructure isn’t new - but the open naming of contractors at the highest level, paired with LGU validation, could mark a cultural shift. If more mayors and governors follow Mayor Vico’s lead, the old “everyone knows but no one says it” culture may finally crack.

As the President said in the #SONA2025, and as Mayor Vico echoed today:

“Mahiya naman kayo.”

In a political climate where both national and local leaders are naming names, corrupt operators may be realizing the game board is changing - and not in their favor.
